title: Cherubim, Seraphim and the Living Creatures
lead: Winged beings who guard and carry God's presence. Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24) and spread their wings over the ark (Exodus 25:18–22); seraphim cry "Holy, holy, holy" above the throne (Isaiah 6:2–3); Ezekiel's four living creatures carry God's throne, and he says "I knew that they were cherubim" (Ezekiel 10:20); and in Revelation four living creatures praise God day and night (Revelation 4:6–8). They are fierce, not the baby angels of later art.

sections.b: Cherubim guard the way back to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). Two gold cherubim shelter the ark, and cherubim are woven into the tabernacle's curtains (Exodus 25:18–22; 26:1, 31). Solomon carves them on the temple walls and sets two huge olive-wood cherubim, ten cubits high, in the inner room (1 Kings 6:23–29). God is "enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1) and rides on a cherub in a storm (Psalm 18:10). Ezekiel sees four-faced cherubim carrying God's throne-chariot as the glory leaves the temple (Ezekiel 1; 10), and he calls the king of Tyre a guardian cherub in Eden (Ezekiel 28:14–16). Hebrews 9:5 mentions "the cherubim of glory," and Revelation's four living creatures recall Ezekiel's.
sections.refs: Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Kings 6:23–29; 1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 18:10; Ezekiel 1:4–28; Ezekiel 10:1–22; Ezekiel 28:14–16; Hebrews 9:5; Revelation 4:6–8

sections.b: Seraphim appear by that name only in Isaiah 6. They stand above the Lord's throne, each with six wings: two cover the face, two the feet, and two are for flying (Isaiah 6:2). They call to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies" (Isaiah 6:3), and one of them touches Isaiah's lips with a hot stone from the altar (Isaiah 6:6–7). The Hebrew saraf comes from a verb meaning "to burn." The same word names the snakes that bit Israel in the desert, which the KJV calls "fiery serpents" (Numbers 21:6; compare Deuteronomy 8:15), and the "flying serpent" of Isaiah 14:29 and Isaiah 30:6. Isaiah describes only their wings, faces, feet and hands, so the shared word leaves open whether he pictured them with snake-like bodies; Jewish and Christian tradition has taken them as a high order of angels (see below). Revelation's living creatures borrow from both visions: six wings like Isaiah's seraphim, the faces of lion, ox, human and eagle like Ezekiel's cherubim, and the same cry, "Holy, holy, holy" (Revelation 4:7–8).
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:1–7; Numbers 21:6–9; Deuteronomy 8:15; Isaiah 14:29; Isaiah 30:6; Revelation 4:6–8

sections.b: Ezekiel first calls the beings of his vision "living creatures" (Hebrew chayyot, Ezekiel 1:5), and later says, "This was the living creature I had seen under the God of Israel at the Kebar canal, and I knew that they were cherubim" (Ezekiel 10:20). Revelation uses the Greek zoa, "living ones" (Revelation 4:6), where the KJV has "beasts"; they are not the beasts (theria) of Revelation 13. Maimonides lists ten ranks of angels, with the holy chayyot highest, the ofannim (the "wheels" of Ezekiel 1) second, the seraphim fifth and the cherubim ninth (Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:7). Christian tradition, following Dionysius the Areopagite and Gregory the Great as Thomas Aquinas sets them out (Summa Theologiae I, question 108, article 6), places the seraphim, the cherubim and the thrones together in the highest of three hierarchies of angels.
